Introduction

Tourette syndrome (TS) is a neurological disorder characterized by recurrent, involuntary motor and vocal tics. It is one of the neurodevelopmental tic disorders and usually begins during childhood, most commonly between 5 and 10 years of age. Tics may change in their type, frequency, location, and severity over time, often following a waxing-and-waning pattern.

Although Tourette syndrome can be socially and functionally challenging, it is important to understand that it is not a degenerative neurological disease. Many children experience a substantial reduction in tic severity during adolescence, although some individuals continue to experience symptoms into adulthood. Associated conditions such as attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), anxiety, learning difficulties, and sleep disturbances may sometimes cause greater impairment than the tics themselves. (American Academy of Neurology)

What Are Tics?

Tics are sudden, rapid, recurrent movements or sounds that are difficult to control. They may be classified as motor tics or vocal tics and can be either simple or complex.

Simple motor tics may include:

* Eye blinking
* Facial movements
* Shoulder shrugging
* Head movements

Simple vocal tics may include:

* Throat clearing
* Sniffing
* Grunting
* Barking-like sounds

Complex tics involve coordinated patterns of movement or sound. These may include touching objects, hopping, jumping, twisting, repeating words or phrases, or imitating another person’s words.

Contrary to a common misconception, coprolalia—the involuntary utterance of obscene or socially inappropriate words—is not required for the diagnosis of Tourette syndrome and occurs in only a minority of affected individuals. (PubMed)

Why Do Tics Occur?

The precise cause of Tourette syndrome remains incompletely understood. Current evidence suggests that it results from an interaction between genetic susceptibility and environmental factors.

Research has identified differences involving brain networks that include the basal ganglia, frontal cortical regions, and their interconnected circuits. Neurotransmitter systems involving dopamine, serotonin, and norepinephrine are also being investigated.

Several genetic variants have been associated with Tourette syndrome, but there is no single gene responsible for most cases. Genetic susceptibility may also manifest as other tic disorders, OCD, or related neurobehavioral features rather than classical Tourette syndrome.

Can Tics Be Controlled?

Tics are involuntary, although many individuals can temporarily suppress them. Suppression may produce an increasing internal sensation or premonitory urge, followed by a need to perform the tic.

This distinction is important because a person who appears to be deliberately blinking, making a sound, or moving a particular body part may actually be experiencing an involuntary neurological phenomenon.

Tics may become more noticeable during stress, anxiety, excitement, fatigue, or particular environmental situations. They may decrease during calm, focused activities and are generally greatly reduced during sleep.

Tourette Syndrome and Other Conditions

Tourette syndrome frequently occurs alongside other neurobehavioral conditions. These may include:

* ADHD
* OCD or obsessive-compulsive behaviors
* Anxiety disorders
* Learning difficulties
* Sleep disturbances
* Emotional and behavioral difficulties
* Social functioning difficulties
* Sensory processing problems

These associated conditions should be assessed separately because they can significantly affect education, relationships, daily functioning, and quality of life.

How Is Tourette Syndrome Diagnosed?

Tourette syndrome is primarily a clinical diagnosis.

According to current diagnostic criteria, a person must have:

* At least two motor tics
* At least one vocal tic
* Tics occurring for at least one year
* Onset before 18 years of age
* Symptoms that are not better explained by medications, substances, or another medical condition

There is no specific blood test, brain scan, or laboratory test that confirms Tourette syndrome. Additional investigations may occasionally be performed when the clinical presentation is atypical, or another neurological disorder needs to be excluded. (CDC)

Does Every Person With Tourette Syndrome Need Treatment?

No.

If tics are mild and do not interfere significantly with daily life, education, social functioning, or physical safety, observation and education may be appropriate.

Treatment becomes more important when tics cause significant physical discomfort, self-injury, psychological distress, social difficulties, or interference with school, work, or everyday activities.

Treatment should therefore be individualized according to tic severity, functional impairment, associated conditions, age, and personal preferences. (American Academy of Neurology)

Comprehensive Behavioral Intervention for Tics (CBIT)

One of the most important developments in Tourette syndrome treatment is Comprehensive Behavioral Intervention for Tics (CBIT).

CBIT combines awareness training, habit-reversal strategies, competing responses, relaxation techniques, and identification of environmental factors that worsen tics. The individual learns to recognize the urge preceding a tic and practice an alternative response that makes the tic more difficult to perform.

Current evidence supports CBIT as an important initial treatment option for people with functionally significant tics, particularly when an appropriately trained therapist is available. (CDC)

Medications

Medication may be considered when tics are sufficiently severe or disabling.

Depending on the individual, clinicians may consider medications such as alpha-2 adrenergic agonists, dopamine-modulating medications, or other agents. The choice depends on tic severity, age, associated ADHD or OCD, other medical conditions, and potential adverse effects.

No medication completely eliminates tics in every person, and treatment is generally aimed at reducing symptoms and improving functioning rather than producing a permanent cure. (American Academy of Neurology)

What About Deep Brain Stimulation?

Deep brain stimulation (DBS) is being investigated and used selectively for a very small group of adults with severe, disabling, treatment-resistant Tourette syndrome.

DBS involves surgically implanting electrodes that deliver electrical stimulation to specific brain regions involved in movement and related neural circuits. Because it is an invasive procedure with significant risks, it is reserved for carefully selected individuals after appropriate behavioral and medication-based treatments have been tried or are unsuitable. (American Academy of Neurology)

What Is New in Tourette Syndrome Research?

Current research is expanding beyond simply suppressing tics. Scientists are studying the genetic architecture of Tourette syndrome, brain circuitry, neurochemical mechanisms, neuroimaging findings, behavioral therapies, medications, and neuromodulation.

Recent clinical and research developments include improved access to CBIT, continued investigation of non-invasive neuromodulation techniques, refinement of genetic studies, and better recognition of co-occurring ADHD and OCD.

The American Academy of Neurology guideline on tic treatment was reaffirmed in 2025, continuing to support individualized treatment, behavioral therapy such as CBIT, medication when necessary, and specialist consideration of DBS for severe treatment-resistant cases. (AAN)

Supporting a Child or Adult With Tourette Syndrome

Education and understanding are extremely important.

A person with Tourette syndrome should not be punished, ridiculed, or repeatedly instructed to “stop” a tic. Excessive attention to involuntary movements may increase stress and make symptoms more difficult to manage.

Children may benefit from appropriate educational accommodations when tics or associated ADHD, OCD, learning difficulties, or anxiety interfere with academic performance. Teachers and family members should understand that tics are involuntary neurological symptoms rather than deliberate behavioral misconduct.

Conclusion

Tourette syndrome is a neurological disorder characterized by persistent motor and vocal tics beginning during childhood. Tics naturally fluctuate and may become less severe during adolescence and early adulthood, although some individuals continue to experience significant symptoms.

There is currently no universal cure, but effective treatments can substantially reduce tic severity and improve quality of life. CBIT is an important evidence-based behavioral treatment, while medications may be used when symptoms are more disabling. For a very small number of adults with severe, treatment-resistant Tourette syndrome, advanced treatments such as deep brain stimulation may be considered.

Most importantly, Tourette syndrome should be understood as a neurological condition rather than a behavioral problem. Accurate diagnosis, appropriate treatment, family and educational support, and reduction of social stigma can make a substantial difference to the lives of people living with Tourette syndrome.
